A create holding Place of origin and Consignee is refused, and each of the six roles belongs to exactly one tab.

conflicts.outcome: The owner's ruling of 5 November wins: an address's roles all come from one group, so an address is listed on exactly one tab (req-1125). The prototype's organisation held once per use is its own seeded demonstration data, where one place is two entries with two ids; the real book holds one record that may carry several roles of the same group, and both roles then show in its Type cell on its one tab. The prototype's category membership (which roles each tab holds) still stands and is cited for it.

conflicts.about: Whether breaking a listed name after its first word is a design rule or an accident of the prototype's seeded rows.

positions.says: In the Name column a name of more than one word is shown on two lines: the first word, then the rest.
Only seeded rows break the name after the first word; a newly added entry renders its name on one line, so the break comes from the seed data shape rather than a design rule.
A row's Name cell shows the name's first word on its own line and the rest on a second line, and a one-word name stays on one line.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype source wins over the trace's reading of its seeded rows: how a listed name is laid out is look and feel, and the design's own rendering breaks a multi-word name after its first word. The real list already does the same, so req-1136 is adopted as existing behaviour rather than set aside. Nothing is overruled: the trace's note still records why the break was once read as a seed-data shape.

conflicts.about: What backs the address book list's Transporter tab: an address type on an address record, or the transporter records the address book keeps in their own right.

positions.says: The Transporter category holds addresses of the transporter type, and a transporter's Type is its own Commercial or Private.

The Transporter tab is a fourth tab backed by the transporters route, not a fourth role group over addresses; a transporter is its own record with no roles and a private-or-commercial type instead, and no seventh address role is added.
The address book stores roles only and does not store an address type, the type being the front door's grouping of roles.
The Transporter tab lists transporters rather than addresses with roles, and narrows by transporter type instead of by role.

conflicts.outcome: The owner's rulings win: the Transporter tab lists the organisation's transporter records, which hold a Commercial or Private type and no roles, so no seventh role and no fourth role group is added and no address ever carries a 'Transporter' label in the Type column (req-2040, req-1135, req-2041). The prototype still decides the tab's name, its place in the order, its panel heading, its columns and its Commercial and Private filter options, so its claim is not overruled: it also carries the three role-backed categories' membership that req-1125 rests on.

conflicts.about: Where the Transporter option sits on the address type question, which ruling:ian-2026-11-06 left to the re-distil: third before Branch, or after Place of Destination and before the divider.

positions.says: Which of the two placements the Transporter option takes is left open, to be settled against the three-option page already built.
Transporter comes after Place of Destination and before the divider that precedes Branch Address.
The address type is the front door's grouping of roles and is what the add flow's first step asks, the roles themselves being asked separately.
The page's four address types run Origin or Consignor, Destination/Consignee or Importer, Transporter, Branch.

conflicts.outcome: The owner's ruling of 5 November settles it: the add flow's first step asks the address type, a grouping of roles, so the prototype's ordering of the six individual roles places nothing on that page and 'after Place of Destination' cannot be met there as written. The Transporter option sits third, before Branch, which is both the surviving reading and the order the page already has (req-2042). The prototype's claim is not overruled: it still carries the option's hint.
